concept.name: Hindsight bias
concept.definition: The tendency, after an outcome is known, to perceive the event as having been more predictable than it actually was, first demonstrated experimentally by Fischhoff (1975). It distorts memory of prior beliefs, inflates confidence in one's forecasting ability, and degrades the quality of performance review.
concept.intuition: After the market sells off, everyone saw it coming - but almost nobody acted on it beforehand.
concept.mechanics: Outcome knowledge reconstructs memory: people recall prior probability estimates as closer to the realized outcome than they were (memory distortion), perceive the outcome as inevitable, and believe they personally foresaw it. Biais and Weber found hindsight-prone investors underestimate volatility and show worse investment performance; contemporaneous decision diaries are the standard countermeasure.
concept.failure_modes: It corrupts strategy evaluation: past trades look obviously right or wrong, so lessons are distorted and the process becomes unfalsifiable. Warning people about the bias barely reduces it; deliberately considering alternative outcomes helps only somewhat.
concept.misconceptions: Hindsight bias is not lying about what you knew - the memory distortion is unconscious. It also differs from outcome bias, which judges decision quality by results rather than distorting remembered predictions.
concept.example: A trader who assigned 30% odds to a rate hike recalls afterward that he was 'pretty sure' it was coming, and carries inflated confidence into the next meeting.
